findings.title: The tech-debt-audit oracle is a Claude Code slash command, not a callable analysis — the baseline harness as described cannot be built
findings.description:
The Overview states the oracle is "The tech-debt-audit analysis skill (forked MIT Claude skill, adapted for squadron, shipped in the 340 analysis pack) is run across projects to capture a measurable baseline of code-quality findings." I verified `commands/analysis/tech-debt-audit.md`: it is a Claude Code **skill** with `disable-model-invocation: true`, frontmatter `name: tech-debt-audit`, a protocol that requires `TodoWrite`, `Task` subagent dispatch, `rg`/`ast-grep`/`madge`/`pip-audit` shell tooling, and it writes `analysis/nnn-analysis.{project}.md`. It is invoked as `/tech-debt-audit` inside a Claude Code session (or via `/sq:analysis tech-debt-audit`, whose `commands/sq/analysis.md` merely tells Claude Code to "Invoke `/analysis:tech-debt-audit`"). Nothing in `src/squadron` invokes it — the analysis pack is markdown copied into `~/.claude/commands/`, and `src/squadron/skills/` contains only manifest/installer/receipts/resolver, no execution path.

The consequence for 320: the "baseline harness" slice ("Run the audit across squadron-managed projects, normalize and persist findings") has no runnable subject. To execute it headlessly 320 must either (a) re-implement the audit as a squadron pipeline/review action — which is exactly the 300-style template authoring 320 says it does not do — or (b) drive the Claude Code CLI as a subprocess per project, which is an unauthenticated, non-deterministic, 5–20 minute-per-repo process the document never mentions. The architecture never states which. This is the "step 3: magic happens" hole under the initiative's *second* oracle, and it is not covered by any Non-Goal.

findings.title: "Join against 300's persisted judge results" has no join key — the keystone slice's central requirement is unsatisfiable as written
findings.description:
The keystone slice's purpose is "The durable home for human sample verdicts **keyed to persisted judge results** (with judge-configuration identity)". The Technical Considerations section commits that metrology data must "join against those results and aggregate **across projects**".

I checked where 300 actually persists results:
- `src/squadron/pipeline/state.py` `StepState` holds `step_name`, `step_type`, `verdict`, `score`, `outputs`, `action_results` — but no result id, no artifact identity, no judge-configuration identity.
- `src/squadron/pipeline/state.py` `StateManager._append_step` hoists only the **last non-None** score per step, so a step running two judges silently loses one.
- `src/squadron/review/persistence.py` writes `project-documents/user/reviews/{slice}-review.{template}.{name}.md` with YAML frontmatter — and that frontmatter carries `verdict`, `score`, `criteria`, `aiModel`, `reviewType` (the template name), but **no timestamp, no run id, no unique finding/result id**. Filenames collide across runs (same slice + same template + same name overwrites).
- `ActionResult.metadata` does carry `{"model", "profile", "template"}`, but that lands inside `action_results` in the run-state JSON, not in a queryable indexed place, and `metadata` is *not* persisted into the review markdown frontmatter beyond `aiModel` and the template name.

So there is no stable identifier a human sample verdict can attach to, and the "judge-configuration identity (template identity/version, model)" the document says must be recorded is only partially derivable (template name + model are recoverable; template *version* and *run* are not). The document asserts 300 "persisted scores as first-class queryable fields and results as self-describing (provenance)" — the score is queryable; the result is *not* addressable. The keystone slice must either add a result identifier to 300's persistence (which contradicts the Non-Goal "No change to the judging path … it does not re-architect the write path") or 320 must reconstruct identity by re-deriving from a mutable, overwritable file. This is a genuine contradiction between Technical Considerations and Non-Goals that must be resolved at architecture level, not slice level.

findings.title: "Comparability across template and model versions" is promised as fixed here, but the existing stack has no template-version concept to key on
findings.description:
The document states: "Metrology records must therefore identify the judge configuration (template identity/version, model) they measured, and reports must not blend measurements across incompatible configurations. … that measurements are keyed by judge configuration is fixed here."

`src/squadron/review/templates/__init__.py` shows the `ReviewTemplate` dataclass has `name`, `model`, `judge` (a dict of thresholds) — but **no version field**, and `load_template()` reads `name`/`model`/`judge` from YAML with no version parsing. `src/squadron/data/templates/judge-slice-vs-arch.yaml` carries `judge: {pass_floor: 82, concerns_floor: 60}` and `model: opus` and nothing version-like. A user-supplied template in `~/.config/squadron/templates/` can override a built-in **by name alone** (`load_all_templates` explicitly says "User templates with the same name override built-ins"), so "judge.slice-vs-arch" can silently change meaning between two measurements with no detectable difference. Since 320's whole premise is that a template revision invalidates accumulated calibration, the architecture must either specify adding a version/checksum field to the judge template contract (a change to 300's template schema, again brushing the Non-Goal) or specify content-hash identity derived from the template file. Neither is stated; "what granularity of identity is practical is a slice-design question" is offered, but the document simultaneously asserts the keying is "fixed here", which overstates what the underlying data supports.

findings.title: Calibration output is described as "configuration" with no writable locus — the mechanism that moves a judge from advisory to auto-gate does not exist
findings.description:
The Envisioned State says "a judge with demonstrated agreement at an artifact level is configured toward auto-gate at that level", and the Design Goals say "Calibration output is configuration, not a new gating mechanism." But the only writable config surface in the stack is `src/squadron/config/keys.py` → `CONFIG_KEYS`, a flat dict of typed keys persisted to `~/.config/squadron/config.toml` / `.squadron.toml` by `set_config`, whose `_coerce_value` supports only `int` and `str`. Judge thresholds, by contrast, live in the **review template YAML** (`judge: {pass_floor, concerns_floor}`) and are resolved per-step by `src/squadron/pipeline/actions/judge.py:resolve_thresholds` (step override → template default → module constant `_DEFAULT_PASS_FLOOR = 75.0`).

Three concrete gaps the architecture does not name:
1. There is no "advisory" mode in the existing threshold model. `enforce_judge` always derives a verdict, and `CheckpointTrigger` fires on `CONCERNS`/`FAIL`/`UNKNOWN`. "Advisory" today is emulated by a pass_floor the score "effectively cannot clear" (300's own words) — i.e. by setting a threshold of 100. There is no first-class advisory/auto-gate switch for calibration to flip, and 320 is told it must not add a gating mechanism.
2. "Auto-gate vs escalate" is not a property of the threshold at all — it is a property of the *pipeline* (whether the step has a `checkpoint:` trigger; see `src/squadron/pipeline/steps/review.py`, where `checkpoint` is what makes a review gate). Loosening `pass_floor` does not remove a human from the loop; only editing the pipeline YAML's `checkpoint:` trigger does. So the initiative's headline outcome ("moving a trustworthy judge from advisory toward auto-gate") is a *pipeline-authoring* change, not a threshold-config change — and the architecture consistently describes it as the latter.
3. `CONFIG_KEYS` has no typed key for per-artifact-level, per-judge-configuration thresholds, and `_coerce_value` would need extending (float is unsupported today).

This is the single most load-bearing unspecified mechanism in the initiative, and it is presented as already-settled.

findings.title: Multi-sample judging does not exist; "the execution machinery exists" is false as of this document's own dependency set
findings.description:
The document says: "The execution machinery exists — 300's multi-sample option and 140's `fan_out` — but running it costs tokens, so dispersion measurement will likely be a deliberate, sampled activity rather than a per-gate default."

Verified against the code: `src/squadron/pipeline/steps/fan_out.py` and `_execute_fan_out_step` exist, but (a) `fan_out`'s inner step is executed through `_execute_step_once` → `ReviewAction` → `run_review_with_profile`, and the fan-in reducers in `src/squadron/pipeline/intelligence/fan_in/reducers.py` (`collect`, `first_pass`) **do not carry `score` at all** — `CollectReducer` emits only `action_type`/`success`/`outputs`/`verdict` per branch, and `FirstPassReducer` returns the first PASS branch's verdict. So a `fan_out` over judges reduces to a verdict, discarding the per-branch scores that dispersion measurement needs; (b) 300's multi-sample judging is explicitly **Future Work 1, unchecked** in `300-slices.eval-actions-llm-as-judge-scoring.md` — "deferred so the core judging path lands first", and a repo-wide grep for `multi_sample`/`multi-sample` in `src/` returns nothing.

So both mechanisms the document leans on for dispersion are unimplemented, and the fan-in reduction path is actively lossy for scores. 320's dependency frontmatter lists `[100, 140, 300]` and the initiative plan says 320 is "Independent of 180, 200, 260, 280" — but dispersion measurement needs either 300 Future Work 1 to land, or a score-preserving fan-in reducer, which is a 140/180-band change. The dependency set is wrong for the stated scope.

findings.title: Judge-configuration identity, artifact level, and cross-project aggregation are three separate keys, but the store decision is deferred without enumerating the join
findings.description:
"Where metrology data lives" defers to slice design: "Whether this extends existing storage or adds a metrology store (and its relation to the anticipated shared artifact store, 280) is a leading slice-design decision."

Three facts the document asserts as fixed but never reconciles against the storage options:
- **Artifact level** is a load-bearing dimension everywhere in the document ("Calibration is per artifact level", "never as one global 'judge accuracy' number", every report is per artifact level). The stack's artifact-level vocabulary is *template name* — `judge.slice-vs-arch` vs `judge.tasks-vs-slice` (`src/squadron/data/templates/`). But the document's examples of levels ("tasks-vs-slice, slice-design-vs-arch, arch-vs-concept") are *relations*, and "arch-vs-concept" has **no template and no judge** today — `src/squadron/data/templates/` contains only `arch.yaml`, `code.yaml`, `slice.yaml`, `tasks.yaml`, `judge-slice-vs-arch.yaml`, `judge-tasks-vs-slice.yaml`. There is no `judge-arch-vs-concept.yaml`. Yet the architecture lists "arch-vs-concept" as one of the three per-level buckets it must report on, and 300's Overview calls it the weak-ground-truth case. 320 is therefore measuring a judge that does not exist.
- **Cross-project aggregation** rules out the existing per-project locations (`project-documents/user/reviews/` is per-project by construction; `~/.config/squadron/runs/` is per-user, not per-project, and `StateManager.prune()` deletes all but the 10 most recent terminal runs per pipeline — a metrology store built on run-state files would be silently pruned). 320 does not mention `prune()` at all, and 300's `StateManager` is a JSON-per-run file, not a queryable store.
- **280 is `not_started`** and its own arch explicitly scopes itself to "structured artifacts written by agents during pipeline execution" with `run_id`/`step_name`/`agent_name` keys — not operator-entered human verdicts, and not cross-project aggregation. Treating 280 as a candidate "metrology store" is therefore a category error as well as a dependency inversion (320 would then depend on an unstarted initiative whose dependency direction points the other way).

findings.title: The pre-emption prompt's "issue classes the baseline actually contains" requires a category taxonomy the audit skill does not emit
findings.description:
The Overview commits to a "prompt-chaining pre-emption prompt — front-loading avoidance of the issue classes **the audit actually finds**". The audit's actual output format (from `commands/analysis/tech-debt-audit.md`, Phase 3) is a markdown findings table with columns `ID | Category | File:Line | Severity (Critical/High/Medium/Low) | Effort (S/M/L) | Description | Recommendation`, where "Category" is one of nine free-text dimension names ("Architectural decay", "Consistency rot", "Type & contract debt", "Test debt", "Dependency & config debt", "Performance & resource hygiene", "Error handling & observability", "Security hygiene", "Documentation drift").

The document's Technical Considerations says normalizing requires "(category, location, severity)". Category here is a nine-value dimension bucket, not an issue class — "Error handling & observability" spans swallowed exceptions, blanket catches, inconsistent error shapes, and missing structured logs, and the actionable instruction to a dispatcher differs wildly across those. There is no mapping from the audit's coarse dimension taxonomy to a dispatch-side pre-emption prompt's actionable issue classes, and no statement of who defines that mapping. Without it, "front-loading avoidance of the issue classes the audit actually finds" is not a spec — it is a restatement of intent.

findings.title: "Audit-findings-per-project" as the metric is confounded by the audit's own non-determinism, and the document acknowledges the confound without resolving it
findings.description:
The document says: "The audit's own variance is itself a calibration concern — the code-quality oracle has the same reliability questions as the judges, and the metrology should be honest about it" and, separately, "The pre-emption measurement is an observational before/after, not a controlled experiment."

Those two statements are individually fine but jointly leave the headline metric undefined. The audit is explicitly non-deterministic (its own skill text: "first run takes 5–20 minutes depending on repo size"; "Repeat-run mode" tags findings `RESOLVED`/`NEW`; "Tuning severity calibration … Edit the Phase 2 dimensions list to set your own thresholds"; per-model "subagents … the main agent merges, dedupes, and ranks"). Counting findings is therefore a function of the audit model's verbosity, the effort-estimation thresholds in the installed copy, and whether the agent's ranking merged duplicates — all of which vary between the "before" and "after" runs for reasons unrelated to the pre-emption prompt. The document identifies "different projects, models, slice difficulty" as confounders but not the oracle's own run-to-run variance, which is the largest single confounder and is the one 320 itself flagged. No baseline-repeat protocol (audit the same commit twice, measure the finding-count spread) appears anywhere — without it, "audit-findings-per-project drops" cannot distinguish a real delta from audit noise.

findings.title: The "cheap human sampling" design goal is listed first as make-or-break but no sampling-offering mechanism is specified, and the available mechanisms are all biased in ways the document itself names
findings.description:
"The capture point must sit in an existing workflow surface (CLI at minimum, honoring interface parity if other surfaces are added), take seconds, and attach unambiguously to the specific persisted judge result being checked. Which results are *offered* for sampling (random sample, disagreement-triggered, escalation-triggered) is a slice-level decision with statistical consequences — a biased sample yields a biased agreement number."

The document hands the *entire* statistical validity of the initiative to slice design while simultaneously asserting the outcome ("Measured trust per artifact level") as a design goal. The problem is deeper than "which slice": every offering mechanism available in the current stack is selection-biased in a way that corrupts the specific numbers 320 wants.
- Escalation-triggered sampling: only judges that escalated (CONCERNS/FAIL/UNKNOWN) are offered — the sample over-represents disagreement, so raw agreement is biased *downward* and no correction is possible without the untaken-rate.
- Disagreement-triggered sampling: requires knowing the human verdict before offering it — circular.
- Random sampling over judge results: the denominator is the set of judges that ran, which is itself gated by the pipeline reaching that step; and since 300's current policy is conservative (judges escalate), the population of judge calls is dominated by the hard cases anyway.

More fundamentally: a sampled agreement number computed on a *non-random* sample of calls is not an unbiased estimate of judge reliability, and the document treats "biased sample yields a biased agreement number" as a caveat rather than as a design constraint on the offering mechanism. Combined with the "honest statistics at small n" principle and the stated reality of "a handful of human spot-checks per artifact level", the achievable outcome is closer to "spot-check triage" than "calibration". The architecture should state the estimand it can actually support (e.g. "agreement among spot-checked escalations") rather than "measured judge reliability".

findings.title: No error-handling or partial-failure strategy for the metrology layer anywhere in the document
findings.description:
The document is otherwise careful about failure modes (it discusses the judges' failure modes via 300, the audit's variance, observational-vs-causal attribution). But it has **no** failure-mode section for 320's own machinery. Specific unhandled cases:
- A human sample verdict is recorded against a judge result that is subsequently deleted or overwritten. `save_review_result` writes to a fixed filename `{slice}-review.{template}.{name}.md` with no run discriminator, so a second run of the same slice+template **overwrites** the first — a metrology sample attached to that result becomes orphaned, with no tombstone or versioning.
- A human sample is recorded against a result whose score was `UNKNOWN` (judge failed) or whose provenance was `review` not `judge`. The document says the metrology consumes "judge-derived vs. review-produced" via provenance, but does not say what happens when a human sample is attached to a non-judge result — it should be rejected explicitly, per the project's "Never use silent fallback values / fail explicitly" rule.
- The metrology store's own write failure. Project convention (`src/squadron/review/persistence.py:save_review_file`, `src/squadron/pipeline/actions/review.py`) is to log at WARNING and continue — a silently-dropped human sample is exactly the kind of data loss that permanently biases a small-n dataset, and no policy is stated.

findings.title: "Advisory" is used as a state in the document but has no representation in the threshold/enforcement model
findings.description:
"a judge with demonstrated agreement at an artifact level is configured toward auto-gate at that level; a judge that disagrees with the human, or judges that disagree with each other, stay advisory and escalate."

`src/squadron/pipeline/actions/judge.py` has no advisory concept: `resolve_thresholds` produces a `JudgeThresholds` (two floats) and `enforce_judge` always returns one of `PASS | CONCERNS | FAIL | UNKNOWN` with `Provenance.JUDGE`. 300 itself describes advisory-ness as a *convention* ("a floor it effectively cannot clear, forcing escalation"), i.e. `pass_floor = 100`. 320 inherits this vocabulary and then proposes a calibration loop that "moves a trustworthy judge from advisory toward auto-gate" — but there is no knob that represents advisory-ness as such, so the calibration loop would be flipping a magic number between 100 and some real floor, and the resulting "graduation" would be indistinguishable from an ordinary threshold change. Given the project's explicit rule ("Never scatter comparison values across code … define it once"), the architecture should specify an explicit advisory representation (e.g. a named `mode`/`escalate_only` flag in the template's `judge:` block) rather than leaving it as a threshold convention.

findings.title: The five-slice plan is reasonable in size but the ordering hides a dependency inversion
findings.description: The keystone-first ordering ("Metrology data layer & sample capture (keystone) … No reporting yet — de-risks the storage/join/ergonomics decisions in isolation") is sound in principle, but as written the keystone slice must resolve the storage/join question that Technical Considerations calls "a leading slice-design decision" — meaning the keystone *is* that decision, and it lands before any slice has validated the join against a real, identifiable judge result. Given the missing result identifier documented above, the keystone risks being built against an assumed join key and then requiring a 300-side change later. The more robust ordering is: (1) make 300's judge results addressable (identifier + judge-configuration identity, decided jointly with 300), (2) capture surface + store, (3) reporting, (4) threshold feedback, (5–6) the audit baseline and pre-emption delta. The audit-baseline and pre-emption slices (the second oracle) are also correctly sequenced *after* the first oracle, and could be deferred wholesale if the keystone proves hard — which is worth stating, since the code-quality half is the more speculative of the two and is not needed to unblock 300's conservative-threshold tax.

findings.title: The document's "no curated dataset" and "no general observability platform" non-goals are well-drawn but the metric vocabulary collides with 300's
findings.description: 300's `criteria` map (reserved optional field, `ReviewResult.criteria: dict[str, float] | None`, populated by the shipped judge templates' `criteria:` block) is a per-criterion sub-score map emitted by the judge itself. 320's reporting produces "agreement and dispersion" numbers, and 300's `gate.py` metadata already carries `judge_criteria`/`review_criteria`. The document never says whether 320 populates the reserved `criteria` map with its own measurements (its Architectural Principles says "Where a latent field exists (e.g. the reserved `criteria` map), 320 populates or reads it") — but 320's measurements are not per-criterion judge sub-scores, they are per-artifact-level agreement statistics. Writing 320's agreement numbers into the judge's own `criteria` map would corrupt the meaning of that field for anything else reading it, and `criteria` is persisted into the review markdown frontmatter (`format_review_markdown`), i.e. into the judge's own artifact. The document should state that 320 **reads** `criteria` (for judge-configuration identity / criterion-level analysis) and does not **write** calibration numbers into it.

findings.title: "Interface parity" is invoked without naming the parity rule, and the tech-debt-audit path has a parity gap already
findings.description: The capture surface must "sit in an existing workflow surface (CLI at minimum, honoring interface parity if other surfaces are added)". The parity rule is `140-slice.command-surface-parity.md`: one slash command per CLI surface area, dispatching on the first word of `$ARGUMENTS`, e.g. `/sq:review code` → `sq review code`. 320's capture surface is a new CLI verb (e.g. `sq calibrate ...`), which by that rule implies a `/sq:calibrate` slash command file in `commands/sq/`. The document's parenthetical "(CLI at minimum)" plus "honoring interface parity if other surfaces are added" leaves it ambiguous whether the slash-command file is in scope for 320 or deferred. Note also that the tech-debt-audit pack currently reaches the user only through `/sq:analysis tech-debt-audit` (a Claude Code skill invocation), while the audit-harness slice implies a programmatic path — the two surfaces for the same oracle will diverge unless the document says which is canonical.

structured_findings.summary: The tech-debt-audit oracle is a Claude Code slash command, not a callable analysis — the baseline harness as described cannot be built
"Join against 300's persisted judge results" has no join key — the keystone slice's central requirement is unsatisfiable as written
"Comparability across template and model versions" is promised as fixed here, but the existing stack has no template-version concept to key on
Calibration output is described as "configuration" with no writable locus — the mechanism that moves a judge from advisory to auto-gate does not exist
Multi-sample judging does not exist; "the execution machinery exists" is false as of this document's own dependency set
Judge-configuration identity, artifact level, and cross-project aggregation are three separate keys, but the store decision is deferred without enumerating the join
The pre-emption prompt's "issue classes the baseline actually contains" requires a category taxonomy the audit skill does not emit
"Audit-findings-per-project" as the metric is confounded by the audit's own non-determinism, and the document acknowledges the confound without resolving it
The "cheap human sampling" design goal is listed first as make-or-break but no sampling-offering mechanism is specified, and the available mechanisms are all biased in ways the document itself names
No error-handling or partial-failure strategy for the metrology layer anywhere in the document
"Advisory" is used as a state in the document but has no representation in the threshold/enforcement model
The five-slice plan is reasonable in size but the ordering hides a dependency inversion
The document's "no curated dataset" and "no general observability platform" non-goals are well-drawn but the metric vocabulary collides with 300's
"Interface parity" is invoked without naming the parity rule, and the tech-debt-audit path has a parity gap already
